I'm not trying to turn anything around. I am not on the side of the police but I also feel that some of these media-hyped situations are ridiculous and result in the martyrdom of felons. There is a lot of gray area when speaking about the current issue of police corruption in society. It's just my opinion that the subject of police training is one often overlooked. Police corruption is a glaring issue today, yeah. There are many corrupt cops that cover up misdeeds and take bribes and are on a power trip. In addition to police corruption, lack of proper training in dealing with situations lead to extreme reactions and that works in either direction. Either the officer is too scared to do anything or he'll just shoot anyone he perceives as a threat. If those are your only two options then your training has failed you. It's amazing that people seem to fail to understand that you can handle a situation in a variety of manners.

How would I have dealt with it? Well, I'm not an officer. I'm an IT freelancer. I also carry a piece because of run-ins with ne'er do-wells in my past experiences. From my experience, if I'm in a dangerous situation I want to stay safe but I also don't want to have to shoot another human being unless it's absolutely necessary. One particular situation which comes to mind is when some redneck fuck tried to pull me out of my vehicle after he almost hit me my car with his in a parking lot. Instead of reaching for my gun and blasting a hole in him, I used pepper spray in his face. That immediately got him off of me and I was able to remove myself from the situation.

In the case of this situation with the officer, he had a taser available. He had a car with locking doors. One of the things they teach you in the military is seek cover before engaging. I feel this officer failed to do that if he allowed a potential threat to get close enough to take his weapon. While the use of tasers in the past was a controversial topic, it has been applied in a wide variety of situations in which it was reasonable to use. In addition, it did not seem like the officer applied many hand-to-hand methods to prevent his weapon from being stolen. In MMA, there are a variety of methods which could be applied when an opponent over extends himself to reach for a grapple. Either the suspect over extended himself to reach for the weapon or the suspect was close enough to grab the weapon. In either case, I can think of a number of tactics which could have been applied. Close quarters combat is highly effective when used properly, especially if the opponent is going for a particular maneuver.

All I'm saying here is that proper training can prepare someone to handle a situation reasonably.There is no need to shoot every single person but there isn't a reason to allow yourself to be beaten to a pulp because you're scared of headlines. If they maintain control of the situation while remaining calm themselves then the officers are less likely to make a mistake. I'm not taking either side here. The suspect in this case was a very real threat and should have been assessed as such. Frankly, I think the officer could have gotten away with shooting the suspect in this scenario and would not have been terminated from the force and the car-cam/body-cam would have backed up his assessment of the situation. But he didn't do that. His training failed him and his own fear overruled whatever it is they teach officers these days.

Also, a further note, if you're a detective and allowed yourself to get sucker punched then something definitely went wrong with your judgement. Detectives aren't you're average officer, obviously. They have years of experience and have likely spent a lot of that working as a footpadder. If he was second guessing his actions during this situation then it seems likely to me that he had time to fall back on his training and properly asses the situation. He should have known better than to let a suspect (who was driving erratically) get close enough to sucker punch him. Indications of drug or alcohol use should have already had this guy flagged as a potential threat in the officers thought process. Again, though, his training failed him. It wasn't corruption this time, it was a failure to properly assess the situation. Not to mention that as a police officer it isn't your job to do what people want, as you put it. It's your job to deal with people breaking the law.

To reply to your claim of "only bad people will take the job", I respectfully disagree. I know a few officers in Austin, TX, a couple of Texas State Troopers, and one TX Ranger. My job takes me interesting places as the company I used to work for did a lot of with with the DPS and other Texas State departments. There are a lot of good cops out there that do their job correctly and are known in their communities. Yes, I think the current police system allows for a lot of bad apples but to say that there are no good cops is a logical fallacy. I feel police corruption is a major issue and I also feel that police training could be better implemented to prevent bad apples. It's a multi-faceted issue where no single thing is the cause for our current state of affairs.
